attributes.title: Level 3

subgroups.name: build 1

steps.hints: ❓ Did you type a number between 1 -15 to set the color parameter in the parentheses in scene.setBackgroundColor(color)?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What code might be placed underneath each comment?

❓ How do you create more blank lines in the JavaScript editor?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Explain to the ninja that typing // tells the project to skip over the text that follows and move onto the next line of code. Just as when naming sprites, it’s useful to be short and descriptive when writing comments. 

💡 Encourage the ninja to use best practices when adding comments to their code. It’s helpful to space out comments in the editor, so that code can be placed in the lines between them. They can use the Enter key to create blank lines between comments. They should also add a space after the slashes in the comment, before adding the text.
steps.instructions:
Begin the project by adding code comments to organize where the code will go in the editor, then adding a background color!


Add comments with these descriptions to the project: set up, player 1 (human), player 2 (computer).


Start each comment with // and add several blank lines between each comment.


Then, open Scene, drag out [set background color to (color)] underneath // set up. Set a color parameter using a number between 1-15.


Click ▶ to see the selected background color appear on the screen!

steps.hints: ❓ Did you add the sprite code inside the curly brackets { } of the controller.Button event?
steps.instructions:
Add a human-spawned sprite to the project when the A button is pressed!


Open Controller and drag [run code on (button) button (event)] underneath // player 1 (human). Notice how the code block turns into JavaScript text:




controller.A.onEvent
(ControllerButtonEvent.Pressed, 
function() {...})

In JavaScript, curly brackets { } are used to create block statements, or indented lines of code that will run inside of another line of code, such as an event or loop. The curly brackets create a “container” for the block statement, like the containers used in the blocks editor.


The controller.Button event has 1 property: Button, and takes 2 parameters: event and handler. In the code under // player 1 (human), use the default property A and default event argument ControllerButtonEvent.Pressed. 


Open Sprites then drag [sprite (img) of kind (kind)] inside the curly brackets { }. Notice how the code is indented when the JavaScript text appears. 

Click the palette to select a sprite image then replace mySprite with a simple name using camelCase.


Click ▶ to see a user-spawned sprite appear whenever the A button is pressed!

steps.hints: ❓ Did you add the sprite code inside the curly brackets { } of the onUpdateInterval loop?
steps.instructions:
Add a computer-spawned sprite to the project!


Open Game and drag out [run code on game update every (period) ms] below // player 2 (computer). Notice how the code block turns into JavaScript text:



game.onUpdateInterval(500, function() {...})

The argument 500 tells the loop how often (in ms) to run the code inside the curly brackets { }. Replace 500 with a new argument to make the computer-spawned sprite appear more or less often.


Open Sprites and drag [sprite (img) of kind (kind)] inside the curly brackets { }. Notice how the code is indented when the JavaScript text appears. 


Click the palette to select a different sprite image, then replace mySprite with a simple name using camelCase.


Click ▶ to see the computer-spawned sprite appear on screen!

steps.hints: ❓ Did you set the minimum and maximum value of possible integers to choose from in randint(0, 10)?
steps.instructions:
Set the human-spawned sprites to appear in random positions on the left half of the screen!


Create a blank line inside the curly brackets { } of the controller.A event. On the new blank line, type the Player 1 sprite’s name, followed by a dot operator . then select x from the code completion tool to add the property to the end of the sprite name. Add a space and an assignment operator (=) next to the property. In JavaScript, a single equal sign (=) is called an assignment operator because it assigns a value to something.


Open Math and drag [randint] next to the assignment operator to set player 1’s x position to a random integer, or number. Leave the minimum parameter set to (0) and replace the maximum parameter with the screen’s width by typing screen.width. 


Then, type  / 2 to set the x position to half of the screen’s width. This will set the maximum possible value to 80, so that player 1 sprites randomly appear on an x coordinate between 0 and 80.


Click ▶ to see the human-spawned sprites appear in random x positions on the left side of the screen!

steps.hints: ❓ Did you use screen.width / 2 to set the minimum possible value in randint(min, max) to half of the screen width?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ Why is the minimum value for randint set to screen.width / 2 and the maximum value set to screen.width? What values does this represent?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Remind the ninja that they can press the Enter key to add additional blank lines on the editor, to add a block statement between the curly brackets { }.

💡 Guide the ninja in understanding why the computer-spawned sprites will only appear on the right side of the screen. The minimum x coordinate will be set to the screen width divided by 2 (e.g. 160/2 = 80), or the middle of the screen, and the maximum x coordinate will be set to the screen width, or the farthest point right on the screen. The program will select a random number between 80-160 to use as the sprite’s x coordinate, which will appear on the right side of the screen as a result.
steps.instructions:
Set the computer-spawned sprites to appear in random positions on the right half of the screen!


Create a new blank line inside the curly brackets { } of the onUpdateInterval loop. On the new blank line, type the Player 2 sprite’s name, followed by a dot operator . then select x to add the property to the end of the sprite name. Add a space and an assignment operator (=) next to the property.


Open Math and drag [randint] next to the assignment operator to set player 2’s x position to a random integer, or number. Replace the minimum parameter (0) by typing screen.width, then typing  / 2. This will set the minimum possible value to 80. Replace the maximum parameter (10) by typing screen.width, so that player 2 randomly appears on an x coordinate between 80 and 160.


Click ▶ to see the computer-spawned sprites appear in random x positions on the right side of the screen!

steps.hints: ❓ Did you select height from the code completion tool when setting the y position’s random integer range?
steps.instructions:
Code the human- and computer-spawned sprites to appear at random y positions!


Create a new blank line inside the curly brackets { } of both the controller.A event and the onUpdateInterval loop. On the new blank lines, type the sprite’s name, followed by a dot operator . then select y from the code completion tool to add the property to the end of the sprite name. Add a space and an assignment operator (=).


Open Math and drag [randint] next to the assignment operator to set the sprite’s y position to a random integer.


Leave the minimum set to (0) and replace the maximum with the screen’s height by typing screen.height


This will set the sprites to randomly appear on a y coordinate between 0 and 120.


Add this code to both the Player 1 and Player 2 sprites. 


Click ▶ to see the human- and computer-spawned sprites appear in different y positions on screen!

steps.hints: ❓ Did you set player 1 and player 2’s score to 0 at the beginning of the project?
steps.instructions:
Add scores to the project to count the human- and computer-spawned sprites on the screen!


Open Info, scroll to the “Multiplayer” subcategory, and drag [set (player) score to (0)] onto a blank line in // set up, underneath the code that sets the background color. Notice how the code block turns into JavaScript text:

info.player1.setScore(0)

The setScore function has one property: PlayerInfo, and takes one parameter: value. Use the default property player1 and the default argument of 0. This will set Player 1’s score to 0 when the project starts.


Open Info and drag another [set (player) score to (0)] onto a blank line in // set up. 


Change the property to player2 and use the default argument as 0. This will set Player 2’s score to 0 when the project starts.


Click ▶ to see both starting scores appear in different corners of the screen.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you add info.player1.changeScoreBy(value) to player 1’s controller.A event and player 2’s onUpdateInterval loop?
steps.instructions:
Change the score every time a new sprite is added by Player 1 or Player 2.


Open Info and drag [change (player) score by (1)] onto a blank line inside the curly brackets { } of the controller.A event, below player 1’s existing code. Notice how the code block turns into JavaScript text:

info.player1.changeScoreBy(1)

The changeScoreBy function has 1 property: PlayerInfo, and takes 1 parameter: value, or the number that the score will change by. Use the default property player1 and the default argument 1 to change the score each time the A button is pressed.


Repeat the process to change player 2’s score, updating the player info in the info.player1.changeScoreBy(1) code so that player2 is selected.


Click ▶ to see how many points the human-spawned sprite can earn against the computer!

steps.hints: ❓ Did you add a timer to the project?
steps.instructions:
Finish the project by adding a timer to beat! 


Open Info and drag [start countdown (10) (s)] under // set up, underneath the code that sets each player’s score. Notice how the code block turns into JavaScript text:

info.startCountdown(10)

The startCountdown function takes one parameter: duration. The default argument is set to 10 in the code; replace the argument with a different value to make the countdown longer or shorter.


Click ▶ to create more human-spawned sprites than computer-spawned sprites before the countdown ends!

steps.hints: ❓ Did you switch back to the blocks editor? What looks similar and what looks different?
steps.instructions:
Test out the project. Does it work as expected?


Switch to the blocks editor to see what the JavaScript code looks like in blocks! Notice what is similar about the code, and what looks different: how do the block statements inside the curly brackets appear in blocks, versus in JavaScript?

subgroups.title: Two Sprite Showdown!
subgroups.introduction: Create a timed clicker game project in JavaScript that uses block statements with events and loops to fill the screen with two different sprites.

validationItems.text: Use the on button pressed event.
Use an on update interval loop.
Use randint and the screen width to set the x position of the player 1 sprites.
Use randint and the screen width to set the x position of the player 2 sprites.
Use randint and the screen height to set the y position of both sprites.
Change the player and computer scores.

attributes.description: You’ve reached Level 3 of Blue Belt! In this level, you’ll learn more about block statements. In JavaScript, instead of adding code into different containers, you’ll add block statements inside curly brackets { } of an event or a loop. Here are the achievements you’ll unlock in Level 3:

badges.title: Thinking Inside the Block
badges.description: Use block statements inside curly brackets { } to add code inside of events and loops.

badges.title: Projectile Manager
badges.description: Create a  projectile in JavaScript.

badges.title: Game On (Update Interval)
badges.description: Use a game update loop in JavaScript.

badges.title: About Yay High
badges.description: Use the screen object’s height property instead of a number.

badges.title: Framing the Discussion
badges.description: Use setDialogFrame to design a custom text box.

badges.title: Settle the Score
badges.description: Set the score in JavaScript.

badges.title: Cute as a Button
badges.description: Use a button event in JavaScript.
